claim: Rap2 GTPase (rap-2) acts genetically downstream of Plexin (plx-1) to restrict presynaptic assembly and to form tiled synaptic innervation in C. elegans.
source: Here we show that Rap2 GTPase (rap-2) and its effector, TNIK (mig-15), act genetically downstream of Plexin (plx-1) to restrict presynaptic assembly and to form tiled synaptic innervation in C. elegans.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding as a main result of the study.

claim: TNIK (mig-15) acts genetically downstream of Plexin (plx-1) to restrict presynaptic assembly and to form tiled synaptic innervation in C. elegans.
source: Here we show that Rap2 GTPase (rap-2) and its effector, TNIK (mig-15), act genetically downstream of Plexin (plx-1) to restrict presynaptic assembly and to form tiled synaptic innervation in C. elegans.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding as a main result of the study.

claim: Both constitutively GTP- and GDP-forms of rap-2 mutants exhibit synaptic tiling defects as plx-1 mutants.
source: Both constitutively GTP- and GDP-forms of rap-2 mutants exhibit synaptic tiling defects as plx-1 mutants, suggesting that cycling of the RAP-2 nucleotide state is critical for synapse inhibition.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this observation from the experimental data.

claim: Cycling of the RAP-2 nucleotide state is critical for synapse inhibition.
source: Both constitutively GTP- and GDP-forms of rap-2 mutants exhibit synaptic tiling defects as plx-1 mutants, suggesting that cycling of the RAP-2 nucleotide state is critical for synapse inhibition.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation that both GTP- and GDP-locked forms show defects.

claim: PLX-1 suppresses local RAP-2 activity.
source: Consistently, PLX-1 suppresses local RAP-2 activity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding.

claim: Excessive ectopic synapse formation in mig-15 mutants causes a severe synaptic tiling defect.
source: Excessive ectopic synapse formation in mig-15 mutants causes a severe synaptic tiling defect.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this observation.

claim: Overexpression of mig-15 strongly inhibited synapse formation.
source: Conversely, overexpression of mig-15 strongly inhibited synapse formation, suggesting that mig-15 is a negative regulator of synapse formation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this experimental observation.

claim: mig-15 is a negative regulator of synapse formation.
source: Conversely, overexpression of mig-15 strongly inhibited synapse formation, suggesting that mig-15 is a negative regulator of synapse formation.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the overexpression data.

claim: Subcellular regulation of small GTPase activity by Plexin shapes proper synapse patterning in vivo.
source: These results reveal that subcellular regulation of small GTPase activity by Plexin shapes proper synapse patterning in vivo.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Semaphorins and their receptors, Plexins, are conserved families of molecules that have a well-established function to repel axons during development.
source: Semaphorins (Sema) and their receptors, Plexins, are two conserved families of molecules that have a well-established function to repel axons during development (Kolodkin et al., 1993, 1992; Negishi et al., 2005a; Tran et al., 2007) and play prominent roles contributing to immune system, cardiovascular development and cancer regulation (Epstein et al., 2015; Neufeld et al., 2005; Takamatsu and Kumanogoh, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous literature.

claim: Semaphorins and Plexins play prominent roles contributing to immune system, cardiovascular development and cancer regulation.
source: Semaphorins (Sema) and their receptors, Plexins, are two conserved families of molecules that have a well-established function to repel axons during development (Kolodkin et al., 1993, 1992; Negishi et al., 2005a; Tran et al., 2007) and play prominent roles contributing to immune system, cardiovascular development and cancer regulation (Epstein et al., 2015; Neufeld et al., 2005; Takamatsu and Kumanogoh, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous literature.

claim: Sema/Plexin signaling plays a critical role as a negative regulator of synapse formation.
source: In addition to its function as a long-range axon guidance cue during neuronal development, Sema/Plexin signaling plays a critical role as a negative regulator of synapse formation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Ectopic expression of Sema2a causes elimination of specific neuromuscular junctions in Drosophila.
source: The role of Sema/Plexin signaling to inhibit synapse formation was first observed in Drosophila, where ectopic expression of Sema2a causes elimination of specific neuromuscular junctions (Matthes et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Sema3E/PlexinD1 specifies sensory-motor connections in mammals.
source: In mammals, Sema3E/PlexinD1 specifies sensory-motor connections (Pecho-Vrieseling et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Secreted Sema3F locally inhibits spine development through its receptors PlexinA3 and Neuropilin-2 in hippocampal granule cells.
source: Secreted Sema3F locally inhibits spine development through its receptors PlexinA3 and Neuropilin-2 in hippocampal granule cells (Tran et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Sema5A/PlexinA2 signaling inhibits excitatory synapse formation in dentate granule cells.
source: Sema5A/PlexinA2 signaling inhibits excitatory synapse formation in dentate granule cells (Duan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Sema5B diminishes synaptic connections in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Sema5B diminishes synaptic connections in cultured hippocampal neurons (O'Connor et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Little is known about the intracellular mechanisms through which Sema/Plexin signaling inhibits synapse formation.
source: However, little is known about the intracellular mechanisms through which Sema/Plexin signaling inhibits synapse formation.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of Plexin contains a GAP (GTPase-activating protein) domain that inactivates small GTPases.
source: The cytoplasmic domain of Plexin contains a GAP (GTPase-activating protein) domain that inactivates small GTPases (Oinuma et al., 2004; Rohm et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Upon activation by Semaphorins, Plexins repel axon outgrowth by inhibiting R-Ras.
source: Upon activation by Semaphorins, Plexins repel axon outgrowth by inhibiting R-Ras (Negishi et al., 2005b; Hota and Buck, 2012; Tasaka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The GAP domain of mammalian PlexinA3 is specific for Rap GTPases.
source: Recent biochemical and structural analyses demonstrated that the GAP domain of mammalian PlexinA3 is specific for Rap GTPases, which belong to the Ras family of GTPases and regulate the actin cytoskeleton (Wang et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Rap GTPases belong to the Ras family of GTPases and regulate the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Recent biochemical and structural analyses demonstrated that the GAP domain of mammalian PlexinA3 is specific for Rap GTPases, which belong to the Ras family of GTPases and regulate the actin cytoskeleton (Wang et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: PlexinA3 dimerization by Semaphorin activates its GAP domain, thereby inhibiting Rap1 from inducing neurite retraction.
source: PlexinA3 dimerization by Semaphorin activates its GAP domain, thereby inhibiting Rap1 from inducing neurite retraction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous work.

claim: Drosophila PlexA and zebrafish PlexinA1 promote remodeling of epithelial cells by inhibiting Rap1 GTPase during wound healing.
source: Drosophila PlexA and zebrafish PlexinA1 promote remodeling of epithelial cells by inhibiting Rap1 GTPase during wound healing (Yoo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Rap2 can inhibit neurite outgrowth.
source: Another Rap GTPase, Rap2, can inhibit neurite outgrowth (Kawabe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Rap2 negatively regulates spine number in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Rap2 negatively regulate spine number in cultured hippocampal neurons (Fu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Rap1 and Rap2 regulate synaptic activity by removing AMPA receptors from spines during long-term depression and depotentiation, respectively.
source: Rap1 and Rap2 regulate synaptic activity by removing AMPA receptors from spines during long-term depression and depotentiation, respectively (Zhu et al., 2002, Zhu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The GAP domain of Plexin is critical to inhibit synapse formation.
source: While the GAP domain of Plexin is critical to inhibit synapse formation (Duan et al., 2014; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a), we still do not know whether Plexin regulates synapse patterning via Rap GTPases at presynaptic sites.
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: It is not known whether Plexin regulates synapse patterning via Rap GTPases at presynaptic sites.
source: While the GAP domain of Plexin is critical to inhibit synapse formation (Duan et al., 2014; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a), we still do not know whether Plexin regulates synapse patterning via Rap GTPases at presynaptic sites.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Sema/Plexin signaling in C. elegans functions in vulva formation and male ray development.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, Sema/Plexin signaling functions in vulva formation and male ray development (Dalpé et al., 2005, 2004; Fujii et al., 2002; Ikegami et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2005; Nakao et al., 2007; Nukazuka et al., 2008, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Sema/Plexin signaling in the C. elegans nervous system mediates a critical inter-axonal interaction for the tiled synaptic innervation of two DA-class cholinergic motor neurons (DA8 and DA9).
source: Using this model system, we previously reported that Sema/Plexin signaling in the nervous system mediates a critical inter-axonal interaction for the tiled synaptic innervation of two DA-class cholinergic motor neurons (DA8 and DA9) (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Cell bodies of nine DA neurons in C. elegans reside in the ventral nerve cord, sending dendrites ventrally and axons dorsally to form en passant synapses onto the dorsal body wall muscles.
source: Cell bodies of nine DA neurons in C. elegans reside in the ventral nerve cord, sending dendrites ventrally and axons dorsally to form en passant synapses onto the dorsal body wall muscles.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Each DA motor neuron forms synapses onto muscles within specific sub-axonal domains, which do not overlap with those from neighboring DA neurons.
source: Even though axons of DA neurons show significant overlap, each motor neuron forms synapses onto muscles within specific sub-axonal domains, which do not overlap with those from neighboring DA neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DA neuron organization.

claim: The unique synaptic innervation of DA neurons creates tiled synaptic patterns along the nerve cord.
source: This unique synaptic innervation creates tiled synaptic patterns along the nerve cord (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Tiled synaptic innervation occurs within most motor neuron classes in C. elegans.
source: Tiled synaptic innervation occurs within most motor neuron classes and may contribute to the sinusoidal locomotion pattern of C. elegans (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Tiled synaptic innervation may contribute to the sinusoidal locomotion pattern of C. elegans.
source: Tiled synaptic innervation occurs within most motor neuron classes and may contribute to the sinusoidal locomotion pattern of C. elegans (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with a citation.

claim: PLX-1 localizes at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain in axon-axon interactions in a Semaphorin-dependent manner.
source: We reported that PLX-1 localizes at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain in axon-axon interactions in a Semaphorin-dependent manner, where it locally inhibits formation of the presynaptic specialization via its GAP domain.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: PLX-1 locally inhibits formation of the presynaptic specialization via its GAP domain at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain.
source: We reported that PLX-1 localizes at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain in axon-axon interactions in a Semaphorin-dependent manner, where it locally inhibits formation of the presynaptic specialization via its GAP domain.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: Loss of Semas or plx-1 causes anterior expansion of DA9 synaptic domain and posterior expansion of DA8 synaptic domain.
source: Loss of Semas or plx-1 causes anterior expansion of DA9 synaptic domain and posterior expansion of DA8 synaptic domain.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding.

claim: Loss of Semas or plx-1 indicates loss of inter-axonal interactions between DA8 and DA9 neurons.
source: This result indicates loss of inter-axonal interactions between DA8 and DA9 neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of previous findings.

claim: Excess dendritic spine formation occurs specifically within the region close to the cell body in the plexin knockout mouse.
source: Consistently, Tran et al., also observed excess dendritic spine formation, specifically within the region close to the cell body, in the plexin knockout mouse (Tran et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Sema/Plexin locally inhibits synapse formation through a conserved mechanism.
source: These findings suggest a conserved mechanism by which Sema/Plexin locally inhibits synapse formation.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the comparison of C. elegans and mouse data.

claim: rap-2 is expressed in motor neurons including DA8 and DA9.
source: Among them, only rap-2, an ortholog of mammalian Rap2a, was expressed in motor neurons including DA8 and DA9, while rap-1 and rap-3 were not expressed in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by expression pattern data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: rap-1 is not expressed in DA8 and DA9 neurons.
source: Among them, only rap-2, an ortholog of mammalian Rap2a, was expressed in motor neurons including DA8 and DA9, while rap-1 and rap-3 were not expressed in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by expression pattern data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: rap-3 is not expressed in DA8 and DA9 neurons.
source: Among them, only rap-2, an ortholog of mammalian Rap2a, was expressed in motor neurons including DA8 and DA9, while rap-1 and rap-3 were not expressed in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by expression pattern data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In wild type animals, synaptic domains of DA8 and DA9 neurons do not show significant overlap, creating tiled synaptic innervation.
source: In wild type animals, synaptic domains of DA8 and DA9 neurons did not show significant overlap, creating tiled synaptic innervation (Figure 1A and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A and G.

claim: In the plx-1(nc36) null mutant, synaptic domains of DA8 and DA9 expanded posteriorly and anteriorly, respectively, resulting in significant overlap.
source: In the plx-1(nc36) null mutant, synaptic domains of DA8 and DA9 expanded posteriorly and anteriorly, respectively. As a result, synaptic domains of these neurons overlapped significantly (Figure 1B and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B and G.

claim: The G12V mutant is widely used as a constitutively GTP-form of small GTPases including mammalian Rap2A and C. elegans RAP-1.
source: The G12V mutant is widely used as a constitutively GTP-form of small GTPases including mammalian Rap2A and C. elegans RAP-1 (Kawabe et al., 2010; Pellis-van Berkel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Expression of a constitutively GTP-bound form of rap-2(G12V) under the A-type neuron specific promoter elicited a similar synaptic tiling defect as plx-1 mutants.
source: Expression of a constitutively GTP-bound form of rap-2(G12V) under the A-type neuron specific promoter, Punc-4, elicited a similar synaptic tiling defect as plx-1 mutants (Figure 1C and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C and G.

claim: Expression of wild type rap-2 under the unc-4 promoter did not affect the synaptic tiling pattern.
source: Expression of wild type rap-2 under the unc-4 promoter did not affect the synaptic tiling pattern, suggesting that G12V mutation but not over-expression of rap-2 caused the synaptic tiling defect (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: G12V mutation but not over-expression of rap-2 caused the synaptic tiling defect.
source: Expression of wild type rap-2 under the unc-4 promoter did not affect the synaptic tiling pattern, suggesting that G12V mutation but not over-expression of rap-2 caused the synaptic tiling defect (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the comparison of wild type and G12V overexpression.

claim: Three independent rap-2(G12V) mutant alleles (miz16, miz17 and miz18) showed the same synaptic tiling defects as plx-1 mutants.
source: We observed the same synaptic tiling defects in three independent rap-2(G12V) mutant alleles (miz16, miz17 and miz18) as in plx-1 mutants (Figure 1D and G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1D and G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All three rap-2(G12V) mutants have comparable levels of gene expression to wild type rap-2.
source: We found a comparable level of gene expression among all three rap-2(G12V) mutants to wild type rap-2 using RT-qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rap-2(G12V) mutation itself, not changes in gene expression, underlies the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(G12V) mutants.
source: These results confirm that the rap-2(G12V) mutation itself, not changes in gene expression, underlie the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(G12V) mutants.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the gene expression data.

claim: The null mutant of rap-2(gk11) showed the same synaptic tiling defect as the constitutively GTP-form of rap-2(G12V) mutants.
source: Surprisingly, the null mutant of rap-2(gk11) also showed the same synaptic tiling defect, as did the constitutively GTP-form of rap-2(G12V) mutants (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1E and G.

claim: Synaptic tiling requires both the GTP- and GDP-bound forms of RAP-2.
source: This result suggests that synaptic tiling requires both the GTP- and GDP-bound forms of RAP-2.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation that both null and GTP-locked mutants show defects.

claim: The constitutively GDP-bound form of rap-2 mutants (S17A: miz19, miz20) showed the identical synaptic tiling defect as rap-2(G12V) and rap-2(gk11) mutants.
source: Indeed, the constitutively GDP-bound form of rap-2 mutants (S17A: miz19, miz20) showed the identical synaptic tiling defect as rap-2(G12V) and rap-2(gk11) mutants (Figure 1F and G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1F and G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cycling between GTP- and GDP-forms of RAP-2 is critical to regulate the spatial patterning of synapses.
source: These results suggest that the cycling between GTP- and GDP-forms of RAP-2 is critical to regulate the spatial patterning of synapses.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mutant analysis.

claim: The synaptic tiling defect in all rap-2 mutants is caused by both the posterior expansion of DA8 synaptic domain and the anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain.
source: Similar to plx-1 mutants, the synaptic tiling defect in all rap-2 mutants is caused by both the posterior expansion of DA8 synaptic domain and the anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: None of rap-2(G12V), rap-2(S17A) and rap-2(gk11) mutants enhanced or suppressed the synaptic tiling defect in plx-1 mutants.
source: However, none of rap-2(G12V), rap-2(S17A) and rap-2(gk11) mutants enhanced or suppressed the synaptic tiling defect in plx-1 mutants (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: plx-1 and rap-2 function in the same genetic pathway.
source: These results suggest that plx-1 and rap-2 function in the same genetic pathway.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the genetic interaction data.

claim: Neither rap-1(pk2082) nor rap-3(gk3975) null mutants showed significant synaptic tiling defects by themselves.
source: Consistent with the expression patterns of rap-1 and rap-3, neither rap-1(pk2082) nor rap-3(gk3975) null mutants showed significant synaptic tiling defects by themselves and did not enhance the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(gk11) null mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: rap-1 and rap-3 null mutants did not enhance the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(gk11) null mutants.
source: Consistent with the expression patterns of rap-1 and rap-3, neither rap-1(pk2082) nor rap-3(gk3975) null mutants showed significant synaptic tiling defects by themselves and did not enhance the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(gk11) null mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All mCherry::RAB-3 puncta co-localized with active zone markers, CLA-1 and UNC-10/Rim in the DA9 neurons of plx-1(nc36) and rap-2(gk11) mutants.
source: All mCherry::RAB-3 puncta co-localized with active zone markers, CLA-1 (Xuan et al., 2017) and UNC-10/Rim (Wu et al., 2013) in the DA9 neurons of plx-1(nc36) and rap-2(gk11) mutants, suggesting that RAB-3 puncta represent bona fide synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: RAB-3 puncta represent bona fide synapses in plx-1 and rap-2 mutants.
source: All mCherry::RAB-3 puncta co-localized with active zone markers, CLA-1 (Xuan et al., 2017) and UNC-10/Rim (Wu et al., 2013) in the DA9 neurons of plx-1(nc36) and rap-2(gk11) mutants, suggesting that RAB-3 puncta represent bona fide synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the colocalization data.

claim: plx-1 and rap-2 act in the same genetic pathway for synaptic tiling in DA neurons.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that plx-1 and rap-2 act in the same genetic pathway for synaptic tiling in DA neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic and expression data.

claim: Expression of rap-2 in the post-synaptic body wall muscle cells under the hlh-1 promoter did not rescue the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(gk11) animals.
source: Expression of rap-2 in the post-synaptic body wall muscle cells under the hlh-1 promoter or in another class of cholinergic motor neurons in the dorsal nerve cord (DB neurons) under the truncated unc-129 promoter did not rescue the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(gk11) animals (Figure 2A, B and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A, B and G.

claim: Expression of rap-2 in DB neurons under the truncated unc-129 promoter did not rescue the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(gk11) animals.
source: Expression of rap-2 in the post-synaptic body wall muscle cells under the hlh-1 promoter or in another class of cholinergic motor neurons in the dorsal nerve cord (DB neurons) under the truncated unc-129 promoter did not rescue the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(gk11) animals (Figure 2A, B and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A, B and G.

claim: DA neuron-specific expression of rap-2 using the unc-4c promoter strongly rescued the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(gk11) animals.
source: However, DA neuron-specific expression using the unc-4c promoter strongly rescued the synaptic tiling defect (Figure 2C and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C and G.

claim: DA9-specific expression of rap-2 under the mig-13 promoter partially rescued the synaptic tiling defect in rap-2(gk11) animals.
source: DA9-specific expression of rap-2 under the mig-13 promoter partially rescued the synaptic tiling defect (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2E and G.

claim: DA9-specific expression of rap-2 rescued the phenotype of anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain but not the posterior expansion of DA8 synaptic domain.
source: DA9-specific expression of rap-2 rescued the phenotype of anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain but not the posterior expansion of DA8 synaptic domain (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: rap-2 regulates synapse patterning in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: These results suggest that rap-2 regulates synapse patterning in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: DA9-specific expression of plx-1 cDNA was sufficient to rescue synaptic defects in both DA9 and DA8.
source: In contrast to the DA9-specific rescue experiment in rap-2 mutants, DA9-specific expression of plx-1 cDNA was sufficient to rescue synaptic defects in both DA9 and DA8 (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a) (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Expression of human Rap2a in DA neurons rescued the synaptic tiling defect of rap-2 mutants.
source: We also observed that expression of human Rap2a in DA neurons rescued the synaptic tiling defect of rap-2 mutants, suggesting the function of rap-2 in synapse patterning is conserved across species (Figure 2D and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2D and G.

claim: The function of rap-2 in synapse patterning is conserved across species.
source: We also observed that expression of human Rap2a in DA neurons rescued the synaptic tiling defect of rap-2 mutants, suggesting the function of rap-2 in synapse patterning is conserved across species (Figure 2D and G).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the cross-species rescue experiment.

claim: rap-1 expression in DA neurons did not rescue the synaptic tiling defect of rap-2 mutants.
source: However, we found that rap-1 expression in DA neurons did not rescue the synaptic tiling defect of rap-2 mutants, suggesting functional diversity between rap-1 and rap-2 (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: There is functional diversity between rap-1 and rap-2.
source: However, we found that rap-1 expression in DA neurons did not rescue the synaptic tiling defect of rap-2 mutants, suggesting functional diversity between rap-1 and rap-2 (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the lack of cross-rescue.

claim: rap-2 functions cell autonomously in DA neurons to regulate synaptic tiling.
source: Taken together, we conclude that rap-2 functions cell autonomously in DA neurons to regulate synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: PLX-1::GFP is localized at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that PLX-1::GFP is localized at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain, where it negatively regulates synapse formation through its cytoplasmic GAP domain (Figure 3A and E) (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work and supported by data shown in Figure 3A and E.

claim: PLX-1 negatively regulates synapse formation through its cytoplasmic GAP domain at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that PLX-1::GFP is localized at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain, where it negatively regulates synapse formation through its cytoplasmic GAP domain (Figure 3A and E) (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work and supported by data shown in Figure 3A and E.

claim: In the rap-2(gk11) mutant background, there is no change in PLX-1::GFP localization but ectopic synapses are observed in the axonal region anterior to the PLX-1::GFP domain.
source: In the rap-2(gk11) mutant background, we observed no change in PLX-1::GFP localization but did observe ectopic synapses in the axonal region anterior to the PLX-1::GFP domain (Figure 3B and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B and F.

claim: The observation that PLX-1::GFP localization is unchanged but ectopic synapses form anterior to it in rap-2 mutants is consistent with rap-2 acting downstream of plx-1.
source: This result is consistent with our hypothesis that rap-2 acts downstream of plx-1 to regulate synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the PLX-1::GFP localization data in rap-2 mutants.

claim: PLX-1 acting at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain regulates the spatial activity of RAP-2 along the axon.
source: Together with our finding that synaptic tiling requires both GTP- and GDP-bound forms of RAP-2, we speculate that PLX-1 acting at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain regulates the spatial activity of RAP-2 along the axon.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the combined findings.

claim: Lower Rap2A activity is observed at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain compared to within the synaptic domain.
source: We indeed observed lower Rap2A activity at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain compared to within the synaptic domain (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FLIM-FRET data shown in Figure 4D and F.

claim: The observation of lower Rap2A activity at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain is consistent with the localization of PLX-1::GFP at the anterior edge of DA9 synaptic domain.
source: This observation is consistent with the localization of PLX-1::GFP at the anterior edge of DA9 synaptic domain (Figure 3A) (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is stated as a consistency check with previous findings.

claim: Local inhibition of Rap2a activity was strongly diminished in the plx-1 mutant background.
source: Local inhibition of Rap2a activity was strongly diminished in the plx-1 mutant background (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FLIM-FRET data shown in Figure 4D and F.

claim: PLX-1::GFP localization to the synaptic tiling border was independent of synapses in unc-104/Kif1A mutants.
source: We showed previously that PLX-1::GFP localization to the synaptic tiling border was independent of synapses, since it was unaffected in unc-104/Kif1A mutants (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: In unc-104 mutants, the same local inhibition of Rap2A activity is observed at the putative synaptic tiling border, but not in unc-104; plx-1 double mutants.
source: In unc-104 mutants, we observed the same local inhibition of Rap2A activity at the putative synaptic tiling border, but not in unc-104; plx-1 double mutants (Figure 4E and G), indicating that Plexin controls local Rap2 activity independent of synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FLIM-FRET data shown in Figure 4E and G.

claim: Plexin controls local Rap2 activity independent of synapses.
source: In unc-104 mutants, we observed the same local inhibition of Rap2A activity at the putative synaptic tiling border, but not in unc-104; plx-1 double mutants (Figure 4E and G), indicating that Plexin controls local Rap2 activity independent of synapses.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the unc-104 mutant analysis.

claim: No local Rap2 inactivation was observed in plx-1 mutant animals expressing PLX-1(RA) or PLX-1(ΔSema) mutant constructs in DA9.
source: We observed no local Rap2 inactivation in plx-1 mutant animals expressing these mutant PLX-1 constructs in DA9, while expression of wild type PLX-1 cDNA rescued local Rap2 inactivation at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FLIM-FRET data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Expression of wild type PLX-1 cDNA rescued local Rap2 inactivation at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain in plx-1 mutants.
source: We observed no local Rap2 inactivation in plx-1 mutant animals expressing these mutant PLX-1 constructs in DA9, while expression of wild type PLX-1 cDNA rescued local Rap2 inactivation at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FLIM-FRET data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Plexin localized at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain locally inactivates Rap2 GTPase to delineate the synaptic tiling border in DA9.
source: While we do not fully exclude the possibility that PLX-1 indirectly regulates local Rap2 activity, these data taken together with the biochemical evidence that mammalian Plexin acts as RapGAP (Wang et al., 2013, 2012) strongly suggests that Plexin localized at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain locally inactivates Rap2 GTPase to delineate the synaptic tiling border in DA9.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion combining the current data with previous biochemical evidence.

claim: In mammals, TNIK acts with Rap2 to regulate neurite extension, AMPA receptor trafficking in hippocampal neurons and microvilli formation in intestinal cells.
source: In mammals, TNIK (Traf2 and Nck1-interacting kinase) acts with Rap2 to regulate neurite extension, AMPA receptor trafficking in hippocampal neurons and microvilli formation in intestinal cells (Hussain et al., 2010; Kawabe et al., 2010; Gloerich et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: mig-15 is the sole ortholog of mammalian TNIK and its paralog MINK1 in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, mig-15 is the sole ortholog of mammalian TNIK and its paralog MINK1 (Misshapen-like kinase 1), which also is an effector of Rap GTPase (Nonaka et al., 2008 ).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: MINK1 is an effector of Rap GTPase.
source: In C. elegans, mig-15 is the sole ortholog of mammalian TNIK and its paralog MINK1 (Misshapen-like kinase 1), which also is an effector of Rap GTPase (Nonaka et al., 2008 ).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: mig-15 can regulate various cellular processes, such as axon guidance and cell migration.
source: mig-15 can regulate various cellular processes, such as axon guidance and cell migration (Chapman et al., 2008; Poinat et al., 2002; Shakir et al., 2006; Teulière et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: mig-15(rh148) hypomorphic mutants showed a severe synaptic tiling defect.
source: We found that mig-15(rh148) hypomorphic mutants showed a severe synaptic tiling defect (Figure 5A and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A and D.

claim: The synaptic tiling defect in mig-15 mutants follows the anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain and the posterior expansion of the DA8 synaptic domain.
source: Similar to plx-1 and rap-2 mutants, the synaptic tiling defect followed the anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain and the posterior expansion of the DA8 synaptic domain (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: All RAB-3 puncta in mig-15(rh148) mutants co-localized with active zone markers, CLA-1 and UNC-10.
source: All RAB-3 puncta in mig-15(rh148) mutants co-localized with active zone markers, CLA-1 and UNC-10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that these RAB-3 puncta represent bona fide synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: RAB-3 puncta in mig-15 mutants represent bona fide synapses.
source: All RAB-3 puncta in mig-15(rh148) mutants co-localized with active zone markers, CLA-1 and UNC-10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that these RAB-3 puncta represent bona fide synapses.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the colocalization data.

claim: Axon guidance defects were observed in 23% of DA9 neurons in mig-15 mutant animals.
source: We observed axon guidance defects (23%, n = 100) or ectopic branch formation (56%, n = 100) in DA9 of mig-15 mutant animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic branch formation was observed in 56% of DA9 neurons in mig-15 mutant animals.
source: We observed axon guidance defects (23%, n = 100) or ectopic branch formation (56%, n = 100) in DA9 of mig-15 mutant animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The synaptic tiling defect of mig-15 mutants was almost fully penetrant.
source: While only half of the mig-15 mutant animals showed axon guidance defects or ectopic branch formation, the synaptic tiling defect of mig-15 mutants was almost fully penetrant (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No significant synaptic tiling defects were observed in cdh-4(rh310) mutants.
source: We did not observe significant synaptic tiling defects in cdh-4(rh310) mutants (DA8/DA9 overlap: 4.6 ± 1.02 μm, n = 21), which can exhibit an axon defasciculation phenotype in the dorsal nerve cord neurons (Schmitz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text with quantitative data.

claim: The synaptic tiling defect in the mig-15 mutants is not a secondary effect of axon outgrowth and guidance.
source: These data suggest that the synaptic tiling defect in the mig-15 mutants is not a secondary effect of axon outgrowth and guidance.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparison with cdh-4 mutants and penetrance analysis.

claim: Two other nonsense alleles of mig-15 (rh326: Q439Stop, rh80: W898Stop) showed identical synaptic tiling defects as mig-15(rh148).
source: The other two nonsense alleles (rh326: Q439Stop, rh80: W898Stop) also showed identical synaptic tiling defects as mig-15(rh148) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: mig-15(rh80) has a nonsense mutation within the highly conserved CNH (citron/NIK homology) domain.
source: mig-15(rh80) has a nonsense mutation within the highly conserved CNH (citron/NIK homology) domain, which is required to interact with Rap2 in both mammals and C. elegans (Taira et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: The CNH domain is required to interact with Rap2 in both mammals and C. elegans.
source: mig-15(rh80) has a nonsense mutation within the highly conserved CNH (citron/NIK homology) domain, which is required to interact with Rap2 in both mammals and C. elegans (Taira et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: A physical interaction between RAP-2 and MIG-15 is required for synaptic tiling.
source: This suggests a physical interaction between RAP-2 and MIG-15 for synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the mutation in the CNH domain.

claim: plx-1 or rap-2 mutants did not enhance the synaptic tiling defect in mig-15 mutants.
source: plx-1 or rap-2 mutants did not enhance the synaptic tiling defect in mig-15 mutants (Figure 5B–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B–F.

claim: mig-15 acts in the same genetic pathway as plx-1 and rap-2.
source: This result is consistent with our hypothesis that mig-15 acts in the same genetic pathway as plx-1 and rap-2.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the genetic interaction data.

claim: The PLX-1::GFP patch at the putative synaptic tiling border was unaffected in mig-15 mutants.
source: The PLX-1::GFP patch at the putative synaptic tiling border was unaffected in mig-15 mutants, even though the position of the PLX-1::GFP patch has shifted slightly posteriorly compared with wild type (Figure 3C and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3C and G.

claim: mig-15 acts downstream of plx-1 to regulate synaptic tiling.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that mig-15 acts downstream of plx-1 to regulate synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic and localization data.

claim: The degree of overlap between DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains was larger in mig-15 mutants than in plx-1 and rap-2 mutants.
source: Interestingly, the degree of overlap between DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains was even larger in mig-15 mutants than those observed in plx-1 and rap-2 mutants (compare Figures 1G and 5D), suggesting that mig-15 also acts downstream of additional signaling pathways (see discussion).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by comparison of data in Figures 1G and 5D.

claim: mig-15 also acts downstream of additional signaling pathways beyond plx-1 and rap-2.
source: Interestingly, the degree of overlap between DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains was even larger in mig-15 mutants than those observed in plx-1 and rap-2 mutants (compare Figures 1G and 5D), suggesting that mig-15 also acts downstream of additional signaling pathways (see discussion).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the comparison of phenotype severity.

claim: Expression of mig-15 under the DA neuron specific promoter (Punc-4c) strongly rescued the synaptic tiling defect of mig-15(rh148) mutants.
source: Expression of mig-15 under the DA neuron specific promoter (Punc-4c) strongly rescued the synaptic tiling defect of mig-15(rh148) mutants (Figure 6A and F), consistent with our hypothesis that mig-15 acts in the same genetic pathway as plx-1 and rap-2.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A and F.

claim: Expression of mig-15 in both DA8 and DA9 rescued both posterior expansion of the DA8 synaptic domain and anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain.
source: Expression of mig-15 in both DA8 and DA9 rescued both posterior expansion of the DA8 synaptic domain and anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: DA9 specific expression of mig-15 under the mig-13 promoter rescued anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain.
source: DA9 specific expression of mig-15 under the mig-13 promoter rescued anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain, suggesting that mig-15 functions cell autonomously in DA9 (Figure 6B and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6B and G.

claim: mig-15 functions cell autonomously in DA9.
source: DA9 specific expression of mig-15 under the mig-13 promoter rescued anterior expansion of the DA9 synaptic domain, suggesting that mig-15 functions cell autonomously in DA9 (Figure 6B and G).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the DA9-specific rescue experiment.

claim: Kinase dead TNIK mutants act as a dominant-negative.
source: Kinase dead TNIK mutants act as a dominant-negative (Mahmoudi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of mutant mig-15(kd) in DA neurons caused a severe synaptic tiling defect.
source: In DA neurons, expression of mutant mig-15(kd), which carries the same mutation at the corresponding amino acid of the dominant-negative TNIK (Figure 6E), in DA neurons caused a severe synaptic tiling defect (Figure 6C, D and I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6C, D and I.

claim: mig-15 functions cell autonomously in DA neurons.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that mig-15 functions cell autonomously in DA neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: DA9-specific expression of mig-15 under the mig-13 promoter in mig-15 mutants often exhibited a shorter synaptic domain compared to wild type.
source: We observed that DA9-specific expression of mig-15 under the mig-13 promoter in mig-15 mutants often exhibited a shorter synaptic domain compared to wild type (Figure 6B and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6B and G.

claim: DA9-specific mig-15 overexpression in wild type significantly reduced synapse number compared to wild type.
source: Strikingly, DA9-specific mig-15 overexpression in wild type (mig-15(OE)) significantly reduced synapse number compared to wild type (Figure 7A, C and D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7A, C and D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduction in synapse number by mig-15 overexpression occurred without affecting the overall morphology of the DA9 neuron.
source: This reduction occurred without affecting the overall morphology of the DA9 neuron (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: DA9 synapse number was significantly increased in the mig-15(rh148) mutants.
source: Conversely, DA9 synapse number was significantly increased in the mig-15(rh148) mutants (Figure 7B and D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7B and D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: mig-15 is a negative regulator of synapse formation.
source: These results indicate that mig-15 is a negative regulator of synapse formation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the overexpression and loss-of-function data.

claim: mig-15 overexpression also significantly reduced synapse number in DD-type GABAergic motor neurons.
source: mig-15 overexpression also significantly reduced synapse number in DD-type GABAergic motor neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of mig-15 under the rab-3 promoter caused severe uncoordinated locomotion in wildtype animals.
source: Further, pan-neuronal expression of mig-15 under the rab-3 promoter caused severe uncoordinated locomotion in wildtype animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Locomotor defects from mig-15 overexpression occurred concomitant with significantly reduced GFP::RAB-3 intensity in the dorsal nerve cord.
source: These locomotor defects occurred concomitant with significantly reduced GFP::RAB-3 intensity in the dorsal nerve cord in mig-15 over-expressing animals and without causing significant axon guidance defects (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reduced synapse number by mig-15 overexpression disrupted proper functioning of the motor circuit.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that reduced synapse number by mig-15 overexpression disrupted proper functioning of the motor circuit.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the locomotion and synapse data.

claim: No significant increase in synapse numbers was observed in plx-1 or rap-2 mutants.
source: Importantly, we observed no significant increase in synapse numbers in plx-1 or rap-2 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the role of mig-15 in negatively regulating synapse number is independent of its role in PLX-1/RAP-2 -mediated synaptic tiling (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The role of mig-15 in negatively regulating synapse number is independent of its role in PLX-1/RAP-2-mediated synaptic tiling.
source: Importantly, we observed no significant increase in synapse numbers in plx-1 or rap-2 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the role of mig-15 in negatively regulating synapse number is independent of its role in PLX-1/RAP-2 -mediated synaptic tiling (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the comparison of synapse numbers across mutants.

claim: Rap GTPase and TNIK are well-known actin cytoskeleton regulators.
source: Rap GTPase and TNIK are well-known actin cytoskeleton regulators (Lin et al., 2010, 2008; Taira et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Presynaptic development requires ARP2/3-dependent branched F-actin.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that presynaptic development requires ARP2/3-dependent branched F-actin (Chia et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Branched F-actin visualized by GFP::ut-CH is enriched within the DA9 synaptic domain.
source: Branched F-actin visualized by GFP::ut-CH (utrophin calponin homology domain) is enriched within the DA9 synaptic domain (Figure 7E) (Chia et al., 2012; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Longer synaptic F-actin distribution was observed in rap-2(gk11) and mig-15(rh148) mutants.
source: Consistently, we observed longer synaptic F-actin distribution in rap-2(gk11) and mig-15(rh148) mutants (Figure 7F, G and I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7F, G and I.

claim: Overexpression of mig-15 in DA9 significantly decreased the length of synaptic F-actin.
source: Conversely, overexpression of mig-15 in DA9 significantly decreased the length of synaptic F-actin (Figure 7H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: mig-15 inhibits synapse formation by negatively regulating the formation of synaptic F-actin.
source: This result suggests that mig-15 inhibits synapse formation by negatively regulating the formation of synaptic F-actin.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the F-actin distribution data.

claim: The length of the DA9 synaptic domain was significantly reduced in mig-15(OE) animals compared to wild type.
source: As a result, the length of the DA9 synaptic domain was significantly reduced in mig-15(OE) animals than in wild type (Figure 8A and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8A and E.

claim: Synaptic tiling is maintained without a significant gap between DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains in mig-15(OE) animals.
source: Yet, synaptic tiling is maintained without a significant gap between DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains in mig-15(OE) animals, suggesting that the position of synaptic tiling border shifted posteriorly in mig-15(OE) animals.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation.

claim: The position of synaptic tiling border shifted posteriorly in mig-15(OE) animals.
source: Yet, synaptic tiling is maintained without a significant gap between DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains in mig-15(OE) animals, suggesting that the position of synaptic tiling border shifted posteriorly in mig-15(OE) animals.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the maintained tiling with reduced DA9 synapse number.

claim: The length of the posterior asynaptic domain of DA8 was significantly shorter in mig-15(OE) animals.
source: Indeed, the length of the posterior asynaptic domain of DA8 was significantly shorter in mig-15(OE) animals, indicating that the DA8 synaptic domain expanded posteriorly (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The DA8 synaptic domain expanded posteriorly in mig-15(OE) animals.
source: Indeed, the length of the posterior asynaptic domain of DA8 was significantly shorter in mig-15(OE) animals, indicating that the DA8 synaptic domain expanded posteriorly (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the asynaptic domain measurement.

claim: The PLX-1::GFP patch at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain shifted posteriorly in mig-15(OE) animals with reduced synapse number.
source: The PLX-1::GFP patch at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain also shifted posteriorly in mig-15(OE) animals with reduced synapse number (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The PLX-1/RAP-2 signaling pathway may specify the position of the synaptic tiling border according to the available number of synapses in each DA neuron.
source: These results strongly suggest that the PLX-1/RAP-2 signaling pathway may specify the position of the synaptic tiling border according to the available number of synapses in each DA neuron (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mig-15 overexpression data.

claim: Synaptic tiling is a mechanism to maintain a uniform distribution of synapses from one class of motor neuron in the nerve cord.
source: We propose that synaptic tiling is a mechanism to maintain a uniform distribution of synapses from one class of motor neuron in the nerve cord.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the findings.

claim: DA8 synaptic domain did not shift posteriorly when mig-15 was overexpressed in DA9 of the synaptic tiling mutants, plx-1 or rap-2.
source: Consistently, we found that DA8 synaptic domain did not shift posteriorly when mig-15 was overexpressed in DA9 of the synaptic tiling mutants, plx-1 or rap-2 (Figure 8B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8B–E.

claim: DA8 no longer senses the reduction of DA9 synapse number in the synaptic tiling mutants.
source: This result suggests that DA8 no longer senses the reduction of DA9 synapse number in the synaptic tiling mutants.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the lack of DA8 domain shift in tiling mutants.

claim: Synapse number was not different between mig-15(OE) and rap-2(gk11); mig-15(OE) animals.
source: Synapse number was not different between mig-15(OE) and in rap-2(gk11); mig-15(OE) animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that mig-15 is not dependent on the Plexin/Rap2 signaling pathway to inhibit synapse number (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: mig-15 is not dependent on the Plexin/Rap2 signaling pathway to inhibit synapse number.
source: Synapse number was not different between mig-15(OE) and in rap-2(gk11); mig-15(OE) animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that mig-15 is not dependent on the Plexin/Rap2 signaling pathway to inhibit synapse number (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the synapse number comparison.

claim: Synaptic tiling maintains a uniform distribution of synapses from one class of motor neurons along the nerve cord.
source: In summary, we demonstrate that synaptic tiling maintains a uniform distribution of synapses from one class of motor neurons along the nerve cord.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: plx-1 and rap-2 play critical roles in synaptic tiling by coordinating the position of the synaptic tiling border.
source: Further, our results indicate plx-1 and rap-2 play critical roles in this process by coordinating the position of the synaptic tiling border.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: Sema/Plexin signaling processes to inhibit synapse formation are well conserved across species.
source: Since Sema/Plexin signaling processes to inhibit synapse formation are well conserved across species, we propose that Sema/Plexin in mammals also utilize Rap2 and TNIK to regulate synapse patterning.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Sema/Plexin in mammals also utilize Rap2 and TNIK to regulate synapse patterning.
source: Since Sema/Plexin signaling processes to inhibit synapse formation are well conserved across species, we propose that Sema/Plexin in mammals also utilize Rap2 and TNIK to regulate synapse patterning.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on conservation and the current findings.

claim: Both smp-1 and plx-1 are necessary and sufficient in DA9.
source: Previously we showed that both smp-1 and plx-1 are necessary and sufficient in DA9, which suggests that smp-1 and plx-1 act cell-autonomously in DA9 and non-autonomously in DA8 to regulate synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: smp-1 and plx-1 act cell-autonomously in DA9 and non-autonomously in DA8 to regulate synaptic tiling.
source: Previously we showed that both smp-1 and plx-1 are necessary and sufficient in DA9, which suggests that smp-1 and plx-1 act cell-autonomously in DA9 and non-autonomously in DA8 to regulate synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of previous findings.

claim: Sema/PLX-1 in DA9 send a retrograde signal to DA8 through an unidentified signaling molecule (X) to induce the synaptic tiling pattern in DA8.
source: We proposed that Sema/PLX-1 in DA9 send a retrograde signal to DA8 through an unidentified signaling molecule (X) to induce the synaptic tiling pattern in DA8 (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is stated as a previous proposal by the authors.

claim: Both rap-2 and mig-15 act cell autonomously.
source: However, we found that both rap-2 and mig-15 act cell autonomously, since our DA9-specific rescue experiment only rescued the DA9 phenotype, but not the DA8 phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the rescue experiments.

claim: Each neuron utilizes a different set of cell surface proteins but share common intracellular mechanisms to specify synapse patterning.
source: We propose that each neuron utilizes a different set of cell surface proteins but share common intracellular mechanisms to specify synapse patterning.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the cell autonomy findings.

claim: Diverse signaling and cell adhesion molecules, such as atrial natriuretic peptide receptor (NPR) and GPCRs, regulate Rap activity.
source: Diverse signaling and cell adhesion molecules, such as atrial natriuretic peptide receptor (NPR) and GPCRs, regulate Rap activity (Gloerich and Bos, 2011; Birukova et al., 2008; Weissman et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: PLX-1 and RAP-2 may locally regulate MIG-15 (TNIK).
source: Considering that PLX-1 regulates the spatial distribution of RAP-2 activity and mig-15 acts genetically downstream of plx-1 in synaptic tiling, RAP-2 may also locally regulate MIG-15 (TNIK).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the genetic and spatial data.

claim: PLX-1 and RAP-2 may regulate MIG-15 activity rather than its spatial localization.
source: While we did not observe a specific subcellular localization of GFP-MIG-15 in DA9 (data not shown), PLX-1 and RAP-2 may instead regulate MIG-15 activity rather than its spatial localization.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the lack of specific MIG-15 localization.

claim: Small GTPase activity is regulated by GAP and GEF (Guanine nucleotide exchange factor) proteins.
source: Small GTPase activity is regulated by GAP and GEF (Guanine nucleotide exchange factor) proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: No significant synaptic tiling defects were observed in mutants of putative RAP-2 GEFs, which include pxf-1(RAPGEF2/6) and epac-1(RAPGEF3/4/5).
source: Yet, we did not observe significant synaptic tiling defects in mutants of putative RAP-2 GEFs, which include pxf-1(RAPGEF2/6) and epac-1(RAPGEF3/4/5) (data not shown) (Frische et al., 2007; Pellis-van Berkel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Multiple RapGEFs act redundantly to activate RAP-2 in synaptic tiling.
source: We speculate that multiple RapGEFs act redundantly to activate RAP-2 in synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation to explain the lack of phenotype in individual GEF mutants.

claim: Synaptic tiling defects in mig-15 mutants was somewhat similar to the combined effect of plx-1 and wnt mutants.
source: Indeed, synaptic tiling defects in mig-15 mutants was somewhat similar to the combined effect of plx-1 and wnt mutants (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: TNIK can act as a positive regulator of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway in colorectal cancer cells.
source: TNIK can act as a positive regulator of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway in colorectal cancer cells (Mahmoudi et al., 2009; Shitashige et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: TNIK integrates multiple signaling pathways for precise synapse pattern formation.
source: While we do not know whether the canonical Wnt signaling pathway contributes to local inhibition of synapse formation, we propose that TNIK integrates multiple signaling pathways for precise synapse pattern formation.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the phenotype and known TNIK functions.

claim: TNIK could activate the JNK kinase pathway.
source: TNIK could activate the JNK kinase pathway (Taira et al., 2004; Fu et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The MIG-15/JNK-1 signaling pathway inhibits axonal branch formation in C. elegans sensory neurons.
source: The MIG-15/JNK-1 signaling pathway inhibits axonal branch formation in s C. elegans ensory neurons (Crawley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: No synaptic tiling defect nor change in synapse number was observed in jnk-1 mutant animals.
source: In contrast to these well-established roles of MIG-15/TNIK as an activator of the JNK pathway, we did not observe any synaptic tiling defect nor change in synapse number in jnk-1 mutant animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: mig-15 does not inhibit synapse formation through the JNK pathway.
source: Our results suggest mig-15 does not inhibit synapse formation through the JNK pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the jnk-1 mutant analysis.

claim: Aberrant neuronal wiring underlies many neurological disorders.
